newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM to seek Japanese aid and investment.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM to seek Japanese aid and investment.

text.p: Bangladesh will seek Japanese aid to build a dam and investment in infrastructure when Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina visits Japan this week, government officials said.

They said Hasina, due to leave for Tokyo on July 1 on an invitation from Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, would also campaign for private capital by offering incentives such as a special economic zone for Japanese investors.
"Economic issues will dominate her meetings with Japanese leaders. She will seek fresh assistance for infrastructure projects," one Hasina aide told Reuters.
He said the Prime Minister might seek Japanese assistance for the proposed Ganges river dam and also for a road-cum-rail bridge to link the southern Mongla port with national highways.

Bangladesh decided to build the dam after a landmark water-sharing deal with India signed last year, with the aim of storing monsoon season water for irrigation and to aid the movement of ships during the dry season.
Officials said the ambitious dam project might cost around 180 billion taka ($4.11 billion).
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria and senior officials will accompany Hasina during the six-day visit that will coincide with the silver jubilee of diplomatic ties between Dhaka and Tokyo.
A 30-member team of leading industralists will also accompany Hasina in a bid to hook Japanese private investments.
Hasina is due to call on Emperor Akihito, meet members of the Japanese parliament and aid officials, and hold talks with Hashimoto.
Bangladesh is one of the largest beneficiaries of Japanese aid programmes, receiving about $400 million a year in grants and soft loans.
Japanese aid mostly goes to infrastructure projects but one Japanese diplomat in Dhaka said Tokyo was now considering giving similar priority to human resource development.
Japanese and Bangladesh officials were expected to sign loan agreements worth $135 million for three infrastrucutre projects during Hasina's visit, officials said.
They were also likely to initial an agreement on protection of each other's investments, the officials said without giving further details.
Tokyo exports goods worth about $350 million a year to Dhaka, against imports of $150 million.
Bangladesh's business community was optimistic that Hasina's visit would help attract much-needed Japanese private investment to the impoverished South Asian country.

"We will again tell Japanese entrepreneurs that Bangladesh would be an ideal place for relocation of their small and medium size labour intensive sunset industries," said Yusuf Abdullah Harun, President of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry.
"Big size investment from Japan is unlikley at the moment but medium and small investments definitely have prospects," said Harun, who will lead the private sector delegation accompanying Hasina.
Officials said Hasina would address an investors' conference and attend a meeting of Japanese entrepreneurs in Tokyo.
Japanese private investments in Bangladesh have totalled $600 million so far, of which $550 million has been invested in the fertiliser industry alone.
A Japanese diplomat in Dhaka said Bangladesh must ensure a stable political climate and radically improve infrastructure and human resources to attract Japanese private capital.

"Political uncertainty has been the biggest damper. Japanese investors want stability in places where they put money. The political situation here is now relatively healthy but still there is room for trouble," A. Takahashi, Minister at the Japanese embassy in Dhaka, told Reuters.

The ruling Awami League, which has passed its first year in office with little political upheaval, now faces threats of disruption from the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) over alleged "misrule" by Hasina's government.
